info: Definite articles (the): Arabic has a definite article, الـ (al-), which is attached directly to the noun. For example, bayt means "house" and al-bayt means "the house." The same article is used regardless of gender or number.

Arabic has three major plural systems.

Sound masculine plural

Add a regular ending:

مُعَلِّم (muʿallim, teacher)
مُعَلِّمُون (muʿallimūn, teachers)
Sound feminine plural

Add a regular ending:

مُعَلِّمَة (muʿallima, female teacher)
مُعَلِّمَات (muʿallimāt, female teachers)
Broken plurals

The most distinctive feature of Arabic. The word changes internally rather than taking a simple ending.

كتاب (kitāb, book) → كتب (kutub, books)
رجل (rajul, man) → رجال (rijāl, men)

Many common nouns use broken plurals, which often must be learned individually.

Indefinite articles (a/an, some): Arabic has no separate word for "a/an." A noun without al- is often understood as indefinite ("a house"). In formal Arabic, indefiniteness is also marked by a grammatical ending called tanwīn, but learners can often think of "no article" as roughly corresponding to English "a/an."

In Arabic, pronouns are used to replace nouns, similar to English. However, Arabic pronouns vary based on gender, number, and grammatical case. Unlike English, where pronouns are relatively straightforward, Arabic pronouns exhibit more complexities and variations. Additionally, Arabic has separate sets of pronouns for addressing males and females and employs dual forms to indicate two entities, a feature not present in English.
